column3: The next ayah completes the antithesis: their call demands disbelief and association, while his call directs them to the Mighty Forgiver.
An answered appeal is joined to steadfast conduct, adding a response-side discipline to the focus's competing calls.
It fixes the Fire as the gathered enemies' destination, clarifying the endpoint of the countercall.
The same speaker warns his people of the Day of Calling, supplying the near narrative horizon for his present appeal.
It identifies rejection of calling on God alone and preference for association, directly explaining the opposed invitations in the focus.
God's rescue of Ibrahim from a literal fire supplies a concrete salvation counterpart to being called toward Fire.
The immediate continuation exposes their invoked objects as unable to answer in either world and names the excesses as companions of Fire.
Failure to answer God's caller leaves no escape or protector, sharpening the consequence of refusing the saving call.
The promised rescue of Lot's household is a general salvation instance, adding little after the more direct fire-rescue contrast.
It explicitly depicts leaders who call their followers to the Fire, a close external parallel to the focus's countercall.
It rejects worship of those invoked besides God and commands submission to the Lord, reinforcing the focus's choice of addressee.
The messenger's call to believe in God supplies a positive human-directed invitation, though the contrast is less exact than the nearby Ghafir passages.
The question about expelling believers and divine help does not materially clarify the two rival calls or their destinations.
Responding to God and the messenger after injury shows faithful answer in action, but it is a broad parallel.
A caller summons people to a dreadful event, contributing an eschatological scene where a call actually moves its hearers.
The prophetic call to seek forgiveness and repent is a general saving invitation without the focus's explicit opposed destination.
Its rebuke for unjust worldly exultation does not add a distinct element to the focus's call-and-Fire contrast.
Distress elicits sincere calling on God and rescue, a lived counterpart to the saving direction in the focus.
The statement about the highest assembly's dispute does not clarify the rival invitations.
Calling on beings that cannot answer until the Resurrection directly contrasts with the valid saving call of the focus.
It places Fire within the consequence of denial, but adds no new account of calling or guidance.
Commercial justice and corruption are not a focused contribution to the competing calls.
The condemned are reminded that they were called to faith and disbelieved, directly linking rejected guidance to the Fire outcome.
The command to protect oneself and one's household from Fire presents the preventative side of the focus's salvation direction.
A prophet warns his people against a fate like earlier communities, a general warning rather than an account of rival calls.
The counsel on spending neither names the saving call nor the Fire-directed one.
It confirms Fire as punishment for disbelievers but is redundant as destination evidence.
It names enduring companionship with Fire after a specific wrongdoing, without clarifying the calls that lead there.
Those formerly invoked besides God vanish at judgment, extending the same-surah exposure of false objects of calling.
It labels the disbelievers companions of Fire but adds little beyond the already established destination.
The prayer for rescue from the disbelieving people is a broad social analogue of salvation.
Zakariyya's private prayer for an heir does not materially explain the focus's contrary invitations.
Fiery assault and the inability to defend oneself sharpen Fire as an inescapable adverse outcome, though no call is involved.
A personal invitation ends with Musa's safety, offering only a distant call-and-rescue parallel.
The disciples answer Isa's request for helpers toward God, a positive response pattern with limited relevance to the opposed destinations.
Its question whether anyone can rescue a person in Fire directly bounds the salvation side of the focus.
The deceiving caller admits he merely invited and they answered, cannot rescue them, and disowns their association: a close account of culpable countercalling.
God answers the distressed caller and removes harm, furnishing the responsive saving pole absent from false calls.
It confronts deniers with the Fire they denied, but it does not add a new calling relation.
A person calls God in distress, then forgets and associates partners before becoming a companion of Fire, joining both focus poles in one sequence.
Sea distress makes all but God disappear from invocation, but this repeats the rescue-and-forgetting pattern already represented.
The Fire itself calls those who turned away, an especially sharp reversal of voluntary refusal into compulsory summons.
The brothers' deliberation after losing hope does not clarify saving or Fire-directed calling.
Those in Fire dispute with leaders they followed and seek relief, showing the relational aftermath of following a ruinous direction.
Those invoked besides God possess nothing, a more general and now redundant form of false-call incapacity.
Pharaoh's wife asks to be saved from Pharaoh, his deeds, and the wrongdoers, adding a faithful model of separation from a destructive authority.
The statement about human stinginess has no material link to the focus.
The creation of jinn from fire does not clarify calling toward Fire or salvation.
The messenger's role as bearer of good news and warning gives only a broad framework for divergent outcomes.
The immediately preceding ayah distinguishes recompense and Paradise for believers, setting the positive destination against the Fire invitation.
Being dragged into Fire depicts its punishment but adds no new directional or calling element.
Invoked idols cannot follow a call to guidance, supporting the focus's contrast between an effective divine invitation and inert rivals.
Answering God's caller brings forgiveness and protection from painful punishment, a concise counterpart to the saving call.
Noah's continuous calling illustrates prophetic persistence but contributes no distinctive destination contrast.
The affirmation of just recompense is too general to advance this specific call relation.
God commands people to call on Him and promises response, while arrogance ends in humbled entry into Hell; it closely joins both focus poles.
It identifies the disbelievers' abiding place as Hell but is redundant destination evidence.
Yusuf rejects a coercive invitation by preferring prison, showing a concrete refusal of a call that would lead to wrongdoing.
God's response to Zakariyya's call offers a general answered-prayer analogue already well established.
The command to call for many destructions in punishment is a late, indirect inversion of the focus's invitation language.
Hell surrounding the disbelievers confirms the adverse end without adding a calling relation.
The same-surah description of Pharaoh's people exposed to Fire and then ordered into harsher punishment gives the focus's countercall a concrete outcome.
Sincere calling during peril followed by renewed association repeats an earlier rescue-and-shirk pattern.
The instruction not to call for peace from weakness is not relevant to the focus's opposed religious invitations.
Ritual worship and submission to one God do not add a distinct connection beyond the established monotheistic contrast.
Wealth and children cannot protect their possessors from God, leaving Fire companionship as a general outcome.
Guidance to right conduct and refusal of association broadly echo the saving side but add little.
The subsequent image of fetters and chains begins the same-surah punishment sequence following the Fire-directed course.
A community calling to good offers a broad constructive model of invitation, now redundant after clearer examples.
A misleading companion turns someone from the Reminder and abandons him, a personal analogue to a false caller.
The people's call to their companion to hamstring the she-camel does not illuminate the focus's salvation or Fire contrast.
The shift to Noah's public calling adds no new element after the preceding persistence example.
The command to guide the associates onto the path of Hell gives a stark contrary direction parallel to being called toward Fire.
Historical destruction for sins is a nearby warning context but does not clarify the reciprocal calls.
Zakariyya's request for righteous offspring is unrelated to the focus's contested destinations.
The messenger calls people to a straight path, a clear positive directional counterpart, though it is a familiar formulation by this rank.
Being veiled from the Lord does not add to the call-and-Fire relation.
The question whether idols hear when called tests the capacity of false addressees, closely complementing the focus's contrast.
The description of a fuelled Fire adds only physical detail to an already clear destination.
The warning of a Fire fuelled by people and stones is general consequence evidence with no distinct call relation.
Associates are set up to mislead from God's path and their destination is Fire, supplying a compact causal path from false direction to outcome.
The question about kindling worldly fire does not clarify the religious calls in the focus.
Those in Fire ask its keepers to call their Lord for relief, a close internal reversal of calling within the very destination named in the focus.
The sea crisis produces exclusive calling on God, but this rescue pattern has already been covered more directly.
Musa's request for ease in his task does not add to the competing calls.
Entering a blazing Fire confirms punishment but adds no new relation of guidance or invocation.
Leaning toward wrongdoers leads to Fire with no protector or help, reinforcing the danger of aligning with a destructive side.
God's nearness and response to callers, coupled with the command to respond and believe, adds a reciprocal model of the saving invitation.
True guardians move believers from darkness to light while false guardians move toward darkness and Fire, a broad directional analogue.
The alleged partners are called but fail to answer as punishment becomes visible, reinforcing false-call failure despite redundancy.
The question about cultivation does not clarify the focus.
Testing upon the Fire describes punishment but not the opposed calls that lead there.
Inhabitants of the Blaze admit that hearing or reasoning would have kept them out, retrospectively highlighting a rejected guidance opportunity.
An inherited practice can conceal Satan's call toward blazing punishment, a direct deceptive-call counterpart even after similar examples.
The fasting regulations do not provide a material link to the focus.
A prayer for its acceptance repeats the answered-invocation theme without adding to the call-to-Fire contrast.
The question about repayment of disbelievers is too general to add a distinct connection.
Calling to the Lord while on straight guidance restates the positive invitation without a new feature.
Treasures and an honorable station have no relevant connection to the focus.
Lot's household is saved except for his wife, a general rescue distinction with limited additional value here.
It states the focus's antithesis almost verbatim: others call to Fire, while God calls to Paradise and forgiveness.
It challenges calling on what neither benefits nor harms and being turned back after guidance, clarifying the error of the countercall's addressee.
The prohibition on calling beings besides God that cannot benefit or harm reinforces the focus's choice between valid and invalid calls.
The true call belongs to God, whereas those invoked besides Him do not answer; this directly tests the rival invitations' validity.
Claimed beings besides God cannot remove or transfer harm when called, supplying a concrete measure of false-call failure.
It presents a decision between belief and disbelief while naming the Fire prepared for wrongdoers, joining direction to its eschatological end.
Those told to call alleged partners receive no answer, an explicit judgment-scene counterpart to the focus's false invitation.
Whoever takes Satan as ally is led astray and guided to the punishment of the Blaze, closely matching a call that moves people toward Fire.
Satan calls his party only to become companions of the Blaze, a direct deceptive-caller parallel.
The command not to worship Satan identifies him as an open enemy, framing the competing allegiance behind a destructive call.
The paired command to worship God and follow a straight path supplies the positive directional alternative to the Satanic route.
Satan's misleading of many people gives the causal counterpart to the Fire destination stated immediately after it.
The command to enter Hell because of disbelief makes explicit the terminus of the preceding misdirection.
Those who disbelieve are driven to Hell and confronted with the messengers' warnings, linking rejected guidance to arrival at Fire.
The same speaker says, "follow me," and promises guidance to the right path: the immediate positive call that precedes the focus's contrast.
The same discourse contrasts the fleeting worldly life with the lasting Hereafter, adding the destination horizon for the two calls.
God protects the believing speaker from Pharaoh's evil while punishment encloses Pharaoh's people, showing salvation and Fire consequences within the same narrative.
The leaders and followers confess together in the Fire that none can relieve the other, exposing the futility of the ruinous allegiance.
Fire's keepers tell its inhabitants to call after they admit the messengers came; their call is declared lost, a close in-Fire reversal of the focus.
The inhabitants of the Blaze admit that a warner came but they denied him, directly supplying the rejected-call history behind their destination.
The command that places of worship belong to God forbids calling anyone alongside Him, stating the exclusive allegiance assumed by the saving call.
